analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate an imported case of Bundibugyo virus infection in a healthcare worker returning to France from the Democratic Republic of the Congo, highlighting the need for vigilance in managing viral infections during travel.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study describes a single imported case of Bundibugyo virus infection in a previously vaccinated healthcare worker returning to France in June 2026, with no secondary cases identified through contact tracing.
analysis.methods: Bundibugyo virus was identified using RT-PCR, and the patient was treated with remdesivir. Contact tracing was conducted to identify potential contacts and assess the risk of transmission.
analysis.main_results: The patient developed symptoms of fatigue, nausea, and headaches while returning to France, and contact tracing identified five low-risk contacts with no secondary cases.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The case underscores the importance of stringent infection prevention and control measures, even when viral loads are low, in managing suspected or confirmed cases of Ebola-related viruses.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings emphasize the need for continued surveillance and preparedness for Ebola-related viruses in non-endemic settings, particularly among healthcare workers.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on a single case and does not provide statistical analysis, limiting the generalizability of the findings. However, the evidence is strong due to the clear identification of the virus and the implementation of contact tracing.

analysis.summary_en: This study reports an imported case of Bundibugyo virus infection in a French healthcare worker who had previously been vaccinated against Ebola virus and was deployed in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The patient developed symptoms of fatigue, nausea, and headaches while returning to France and was treated with remdesivir, resulting in full recovery. Contact tracing identified five low-risk contacts, with no secondary cases detected. The case highlights the importance of stringent infection prevention and control measures, even with low viral loads, when managing suspected or confirmed cases of Ebola-related viruses. The study's findings have implications for surveillance and preparedness in non-endemic settings, particularly for healthcare workers. However, the study is limited by its focus on a single case and the absence of statistical analysis, which affects the generalizability of the results.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在调查一名从刚果民主共和国返回法国的医护人员感染本迪布焦病毒的输入性病例,强调在旅行期间管理病毒感染时保持警惕的必要性。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究描述了一名输入性本迪布焦病毒感染病例,该病例是一名于 2026 年 6 月返回法国的先前接种过疫苗的医护人员,通过接触者追踪未发现继发病例。
elements_zh.methods: 通过 RT-PCR 鉴定出本迪布焦病毒,该患者接受了瑞德西韦治疗。进行接触者追踪是为了识别潜在接触者并评估 传播 的风险。
elements_zh.main_results: 该患者在返回法国时出现疲劳、恶心和头痛的症状,接触者追踪发现了五名低风险接触者,没有继发病例。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 该病例凸显了即使在病毒载量较低的情况下,严格的感染预防和控制措施在管理埃博拉相关病毒疑似或确诊病例方面的重要性。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果强调,在非流行环境中,特别是在医护人员中,需要继续采取 监测 措施并为埃博拉相关病毒做好准备。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究基于单个案例,不提供统计分析,限制了研究结果的普遍性。然而,由于病毒的明确识别和接触者追踪的实施,证据是强有力的。

papers.title: Identification of Probable New Anti-Ebola Virus Drugs
papers.abstract: This work is about finding probable new anti-Ebola drugs. A formula [1] is used for that purpose- (Log A/Log B) =64.5/C-H-N-O. Where, C-H-N-O is molecular weight of the Ebola virus antigens. This formula was used to identify probable new anti-HIV drugs [2] and the cause of dementia [3]. Use of the formula [1] -(Log A/Log B) =64.5/C-H-N-O, to identify the constitution of probable anti Ebola drugs. “Log A is Logarithm of molecular weight (elemental atomic weight multiplied by number of molecules of that element) of individual element(s) of drug. Log B is Logarithm of molecular weight of similar element(s) of Deoxy Ribose Nucleic Acid (DNA). C-H-N-O is basic effector. 64.5 Kda is the molecular weight of a complex effector molecule-Haemoglobin. Atomic weight of the element x number of molecules of the same molecule = Molecular weight of that element in either DNA or Drug” [1].
papers.journal: Saudi Journal of Medical and Pharmaceutical Sciences

papers.title: Ebola in the DRC: A different problem compounded by violence
papers.abstract: A Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC) has been declared in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) due to Ebola disease from Bundibugyo virus. Non-health-focused factors should be fundamental to how DRC and its partners respond to and recover from the current emergency. Filovirus emergencies are violent in every sense—the disease experience of patients and their caregivers, the tumult in impacted communities, sometimes the physical manifestations of frustration against healthcare services, the fits and starts of concerted response, and the milieu of conflict in which this emergency occurred. Yet, interpersonal and organized violence may contribute to frequency of health emergencies and delays in responding to them. We tend to focus on immediate, direct health needs when managing risks from emerging infectious diseases. Sustained success, though, requires concomitant action on both health and non-health aspects of emergencies and the contexts in which they arise.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addresses the need to understand how non-health factors contribute to the complexity of managing Ebola disease outbreaks, particularly in the context of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). The declared Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC) highlights the urgency of addressing these multifaceted challenges.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study is a qualitative analysis of the Ebola disease outbreak in the DRC, focusing on the interplay between health and non-health factors. It examines the impact of violence on the outbreak's management and the broader socio-political context in which it occurred.
analysis.methods: The methods involve a review of the socio-political and health-related factors influencing the Ebola outbreak in the DRC, including the role of violence in complicating public health responses and the broader context of the emergency.
analysis.main_results: The study found that interpersonal and organized violence significantly contribute to the frequency and challenges of health emergencies, as well as delays in responding to them in the DRC.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that the focus on immediate health needs during outbreaks may overlook the critical role of non-health factors, such as violence, in shaping the emergency's trajectory. This insight is novel in highlighting the need for integrated approaches to outbreak management.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the importance of addressing non-health factors in public health emergencies, particularly in conflict-affected regions, to improve response effectiveness and prevent future outbreaks.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on qualitative analysis and abstract-level reporting, which may lack the depth of quantitative data. However, the evidence is strong given the context of the declared PHEIC and the explicit focus on the DRC's socio-political environment.

analysis.summary_en: This study examines the role of non-health factors, particularly violence, in exacerbating the challenges of managing the Ebola disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). It highlights that the outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo virus, is compounded by interpersonal and organized violence, which affects both the disease experience and the response efforts. The authors argue that addressing these non-health aspects is essential for effective outbreak management, as focusing solely on health needs may overlook critical contextual influences. The study underscores the need for integrated approaches that consider both health and socio-political factors in public health emergencies. While the evidence is based on abstract-level reporting, it is supported by the declaration of a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC) and the specific context of the DRC. The findings suggest that future responses should include concomitant action on health and non-health dimensions to achieve sustained success in managing such crises.

elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究对刚果民主共和国的埃博拉病毒 暴发 进行定性分析,重点关注健康因素和非健康因素之间的相互作用。它研究了暴力对 暴发 管理的影响以及暴力发生的更广泛的社会政治背景。
elements_zh.methods: 这些方法涉及对影响刚果民主共和国埃博拉病毒 暴发 的社会政治和健康相关因素进行审查,包括暴力在使公共卫生应对措施复杂化方面的作用以及更广泛的紧急情况。
elements_zh.main_results: 研究发现,人际暴力和有组织暴力在很大程度上导致了刚果民主共和国突发卫生事件的发生频率和挑战,以及应对突发事件的延迟。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,暴发 期间对当前卫生需求的关注可能会忽视暴力等非健康因素在塑造紧急情况轨迹中的关键作用。这一见解的新颖之处在于强调了对 暴发 管理的集成方法的需求。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,必须解决突发公共卫生事件中的非健康因素,特别是在受冲突影响的地区,以提高应对有效性并预防未来的 暴发。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究因其依赖定性分析和抽象报告而受到限制,可能缺乏定量数据的深度。然而,考虑到宣布的国际公共卫生紧急事件的背景以及对刚果民主共和国社会政治环境的明确关注,证据是强有力的。

analysis.summary_en: This scoping review evaluates the role of water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services in Ebola virus disease (EVD) preparedness and response across Uganda, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and South Sudan. Using PRISMA-ScR-guided methods, it synthesised 41 sources from 2014–2026 across multiple databases. The review concludes that robust WASH infrastructure—including reliable water supplies, sanitation facilities, handwashing stations, environmental cleaning and waste management—supports effective infection control during outbreaks. Uganda exhibited stronger surveillance and rapid-response systems, whereas the DRC faced persistent facility-level weaknesses despite extensive outbreak experience, and South Sudan grappled with structural and humanitarian constraints. Key gaps include inadequate infrastructure, insufficient supplies, limited training and weak maintenance systems, alongside over-reliance on temporary external assistance. The review recommends embedding WASH preparedness into routine health-system planning, strengthening maintenance, and enhancing community engagement and cross-border coordination to improve outbreak resilience.

elements_zh.scope_and_question: 该审查审查了乌干达、刚果民主共和国 (DRC) 和南苏丹的 暴发 或 暴发 (EVD) 期间水、环境卫生和个人卫生 (WASH) 服务在感染预防和控制中的作用,重点关注脆弱和 暴发 易发环境的准备和应对。
elements_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 本次范围界定审查遵循 PRISMA-ScR 指南,并使用 PubMed、African Index Medicus、Google Scholar、African Journals Online (AJOL) 和 WHO IRIS 存储库检索了 2014 年至 2026 年期间发表的文献。有关这三个国家的 WASH、感染预防和控制、埃博拉病毒准备或应对的同行评审和灰色文献来源均符合资格。经过重复数据删除和资格评估后,41 个独特的来源被纳入并按主题进行综合。
elements_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 可靠的供水、卫生设施、洗手站、环境清洁和废物管理系统始终被认为支持埃博拉 暴发 期间有效的感染控制实践。乌干达表现出相对较强的 监测 和快速响应安排,而刚果民主共和国表现出丰富的 暴发 经验,但设施层面持续存在弱点。南苏丹面临严重的结构性和人道主义限制,阻碍了准备工作。
elements_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 由于基础设施不足、防护用品不足、实践培训有限、维护系统薄弱以及依赖临时外部援助,准备工作受到削弱。该审查强调需要进一步进行比较和针对具体国家的研究,以衡量 WASH 干预措施的独立贡献和长期功能。
elements_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 可持续的埃博拉防备需要将 WASH 基础设施、实用的医护人员培训、社区参与和跨境协调纳入常规卫生系统规划和融资。加强维护系统和减少对临时外部援助的依赖是关键优先事项。

papers.title_zh: 南苏丹、乌干达和刚果民主共和国埃博拉病毒防范和应对中的水、环境卫生和个人卫生:范围界定审查
papers.source_body_en: Water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services are fundamental to infection prevention and control during Ebola virus disease outbreaks. However, their contribution to outbreak preparedness and response remains insufficiently synthesised, particularly in fragile and outbreak-prone settings. This scoping review examined the importance of WASH in Ebola preparedness and response in Uganda, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and South Sudan. The review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). Literature published between 2014 and 2026 was searched through PubMed, African Index Medicus, Google Scholar, African Journals Online (AJOL) and the World Health Organization Institutional Repository for Information Sharing (IRIS). Peer-reviewed and grey-literature sources addressing WASH, infection prevention and control, preparedness or response to Ebola in the three countries were considered. The evidence was charted and synthesised thematically. The searches displayed 1,963 results, of which 861 were captured for title, abstract, summary or full-text screening. After eligibility assessment and cross-platform deduplication, 41 unique sources were included. Six themes emerged: WASH infrastructure and service readiness; infection prevention and control preparedness; healthcare-worker preparedness; community engagement and risk communication; cross-border surveillance and institutional coordination; and institutional, financial and logistical constraints. Reliable water supplies, sanitation facilities, handwashing stations, environmental cleaning and waste-management systems supported effective infection-control practices. Nevertheless, preparedness was weakened by inadequate infrastructure, insufficient protective supplies, limited practical training, weak maintenance systems and dependence on temporary external assistance. Uganda demonstrated comparatively stronger surveillance and rapid-response arrangements; the DRC had extensive outbreak experience but persistent facility-level weaknesses, while South Sudan faced substantial structural and humanitarian constraints. Sustainable Ebola preparedness requires WASH infrastructure, practical healthcare-worker training, community participation and cross-border coordination to be incorporated into routine health-system planning and financing. Further comparative and country-specific research is required to measure the independent contribution and long-term functionality of WASH interventions.

analysis_zh.scope_and_question: 该审查审查了乌干达、刚果民主共和国 (DRC) 和南苏丹的 暴发 或 暴发 (EVD) 期间水、环境卫生和个人卫生 (WASH) 服务在感染预防和控制中的作用,重点关注脆弱和 暴发 易发环境的准备和应对。
analysis_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 本次范围界定审查遵循 PRISMA-ScR 指南,并使用 PubMed、African Index Medicus、Google Scholar、African Journals Online (AJOL) 和 WHO IRIS 存储库检索了 2014 年至 2026 年期间发表的文献。有关这三个国家的 WASH、感染预防和控制、埃博拉病毒准备或应对的同行评审和灰色文献来源均符合资格。经过重复数据删除和资格评估后,41 个独特的来源被纳入并按主题进行综合。
analysis_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 可靠的供水、卫生设施、洗手站、环境清洁和废物管理系统始终被认为支持埃博拉 暴发 期间有效的感染控制实践。乌干达表现出相对较强的 监测 和快速响应安排,而刚果民主共和国表现出丰富的 暴发 经验,但设施层面持续存在弱点。南苏丹面临严重的结构性和人道主义限制,阻碍了准备工作。
analysis_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 由于基础设施不足、防护用品不足、实践培训有限、维护系统薄弱以及依赖临时外部援助,准备工作受到削弱。该审查强调需要进一步进行比较和针对具体国家的研究,以衡量 WASH 干预措施的独立贡献和长期功能。
analysis_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 可持续的埃博拉防备需要将 WASH 基础设施、实用的医护人员培训、社区参与和跨境协调纳入常规卫生系统规划和融资。加强维护系统和减少对临时外部援助的依赖是关键优先事项。

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addresses why community resistance to Ebola treatment centres in Ituri province, DRC, emerged during the Bundibugyo Ebola virus outbreak, highlighting gaps in risk communication and community engagement despite advances in outbreak control.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The paper synthesizes recent reports and comparative evidence from the West African Ebola epidemic to examine determinants of community resistance to Ebola treatment centres in Ituri province, DRC.
analysis.methods: The authors review qualitative reports and secondary evidence describing community perceptions and mistrust related to Ebola treatment centres, focusing on early distrust dynamics observed in Sierra Leone.
analysis.main_results: Communities feared that patients admitted to Ebola treatment centres would not return, reflecting mistrust, uncertainty, and perceived exclusion from decision-making processes.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret resistance as driven by social and communication failures rather than clinical or logistical shortcomings, emphasizing the need to prioritize risk communication and community engagement alongside biomedical interventions.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings caution that without addressing community trust and engagement, even effective diagnostics and treatments may fail to control Ebola outbreaks due to resistance to treatment centres.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is limited to qualitative reports and secondary comparisons, lacking primary data collection or quantitative analysis, which constrains the strength of conclusions and generalisability.

analysis.summary_en: This study examines why communities in Ituri province, Democratic Republic of the Congo, resisted Ebola treatment centres during the Bundibugyo Ebola virus outbreak, attributing resistance to mistrust, uncertainty, and perceived exclusion from decision-making. Drawing on reports from Sierra Leone, the authors argue that distrust in treatment centres emerged early in the West African epidemic, with communities fearing patients would not return. They conclude that risk communication and community engagement are as critical as biomedical interventions for outbreak control. However, the evidence relies on qualitative reports and secondary comparisons without primary data or quantitative analysis, limiting the strength and generalisability of the findings.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究探讨了刚果民主共和国伊图里省埃博拉 治疗 中心为何在 Bundibugyo 埃博拉病毒 暴发 期间出现社区抵抗的原因,强调尽管 暴发 控制取得了进展,但风险沟通和社区参与方面仍存在差距。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本文综合了西非埃博拉疫情的最新报告和比较证据,以研究刚果民主共和国伊图里省埃博拉 治疗 中心社区抵抗力的决定因素。
elements_zh.methods: 作者回顾了描述社区对埃博拉 治疗 中心相关看法和不信任的定性报告和二手证据,重点关注在塞拉利昂观察到的早期不信任动态。
elements_zh.main_results: 社区担心埃博拉 治疗 中心收治的患者不会返回,这反映出不信任、不确定性以及被认为被排除在决策过程之外。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将阻力解释为由社会和沟通失败而非临床或后勤缺陷驱动,强调需要优先考虑风险沟通和社区参与以及生物医学干预措施。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果警告说,如果不解决社区信任和参与问题,即使有效的诊断和 治疗 也可能因对 治疗 中心的抵抗而无法控制埃博拉病毒 治疗。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 证据仅限于定性报告和次要比较,缺乏主要数据收集或定量分析,这限制了结论的力度和普遍性。

papers.full_text: On 4 September 2025, the Ministry of Health of the Democratic Republic of the Congo declared an outbreak of Ebola virus disease in Kasai Province after laboratory testing at the National Institute of Biomedical Research in Kinshasa confirmed infection with Ebola virus, species Orthoebolavirus zairense [1]. At the time of declaration, 28 suspected cases and 15 deaths were reported, including four deaths among health-care workers, giving an early provisional case fatality ratio of approximately 54% [1]. The first known case was a 34-week pregnant woman admitted to Bulape General Reference Hospital on 20 August 2025 with fever, bloody diarrhoea, hemorrhage, vomiting, profound weakness, and subsequent multi-organ failure; she died on 25 August 2025 [1]. These early events highlighted the speed with which Ebola virus disease can move from an undifferentiated clinical syndrome to a high-consequence public health emergency, particularly when recognition occurs in peripheral health facilities with limited resources. Subsequent surveillance refined the epidemiological picture. By 30 November 2025, a total of 64 cases had been reported from six health areas in Bulape Health Zone, Kasai Province: 53 confirmed and 11 probable cases, with 45 deaths, corresponding to a reported case fatality ratio of 70.3% [2]. The outbreak was declared over on 1 December 2025 after 42 days had passed without new cases since the last confirmed patient tested negative and was discharged on 19 October 2025 [2, 3]. This final reporting is important because early outbreak figures are necessarily provisional and may change as case finding, laboratory confirmation, retrospective classification, and death investigations progress. The 2025 Kasai outbreak was the sixteenth Ebola virus disease outbreak reported in the Democratic Republic of the Congo since Ebola was first identified in 1976 [2, 3]. Although the outbreak was ultimately contained within approximately three months, it resulted in substantial mortality and again demonstrated the vulnerability of remote health systems facing a highly lethal viral haemorrhagic fever. WHO initially assessed the public health risk as high at the national level, moderate at the regional level, and low at the global level [1]. This risk assessment remains an appropriate framing: the outbreak did not represent an imminent global spread scenario, but it did constitute a serious national and regional preparedness challenge with wider implications for global health security. Several features made the outbreak particularly concerning. Bulape Health Zone is a rural and difficult-to-access area, where transport, communication, laboratory referral, and clinical evacuation can be delayed [2, 4]. These operational constraints can slow case detection, isolation, safe referral, contact tracing, and safe and dignified burial practices. WHO reported that early transmission involved health-care-associated exposure and a high-transmission funeral event, both of which are well-recognized drivers of Ebola amplification [2]. Such patterns underline the importance of early clinical suspicion, immediate infection prevention and control measures, and community engagement from the first signs of a suspected cluster. Health-worker infections were among the most important signals of system vulnerability. Final WHO reporting documented five health-worker cases, including four nurses and one laboratory technician, three of whom died [2]. These infections should not be viewed only as occupational tragedies; they are also warning indicators of gaps in triage, personal protective equipment availability, infection prevention and control training, environmental hygiene, and early diagnostic pathways. In Ebola outbreaks, protecting health workers is central to protecting communities, because health facilities can either interrupt transmission or become sites of amplification. The response to the Kasai outbreak also illustrates how Ebola preparedness has evolved. The Ministry of Health, supported by WHO and partners, strengthened coordination, surveillance, laboratory diagnosis, case management, vaccination, infection prevention and control, safe burials, and risk communication [2, 3]. WHO deployed experts and frontline responders, delivered medical supplies and equipment, and supported mobile laboratory capacity to reduce diagnostic delays [2]. These measures cannot reverse the losses experienced by affected families and communities, but they likely contributed to interrupting transmission and limiting geographic spread. Vaccination was a major component of the response. Ebola vaccination began in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in September 2025 using the rVSVΔG-ZEBOV-GP vaccine, also known as Ervebo, initially targeting contacts, contacts of contacts, and frontline workers [5]. By the final outbreak report, 47,577 people had been vaccinated, including contacts, potential contacts, and at-risk individuals in affected areas [2]. The use of ring vaccination in Kasai was supported by evidence from previous Ebola responses, including the Guinea ring-vaccination trial, which demonstrated that rVSV-vectored vaccination could substantially reduce Ebola virus disease risk when deployed around confirmed cases and their contacts [6]. Further evidence from the Democratic Republic of the Congo has strengthened the case for rapid ring vaccination as part of an integrated outbreak-control strategy [7]. Therapeutic readiness has also improved compared with earlier Ebola outbreaks. During the Kasai response, patients received monoclonal antibody therapy as part of clinical management [2]. This reflects evidence from the PALM trial, which showed improved survival among patients treated with monoclonal antibody therapies compared with earlier investigational regimens [8]. WHO guidelines subsequently issued strong recommendations for monoclonal antibody therapies for Ebola virus disease caused by Ebola virus, when delivered alongside optimized supportive care [9]. Nevertheless, the high case fatality ratio in Kasai shows that the availability of therapeutics alone is insufficient. Survival depends on early presentation, rapid diagnosis, safe referral, adequate supportive care, timely treatment, and community trust in the response. The outbreak also reinforces the value of genomic surveillance. Whole-genome sequencing of early confirmed cases suggested that the 2025 Kasai outbreak was most likely caused by a new zoonotic spillover event rather than direct continuation of previous Kasai outbreaks [2]. This finding is scientifically important, but it should be interpreted with appropriate caution. Genomic inference depends on the completeness of sampling, the quality and timeliness of sequencing, and the availability of comparator genomes. Genomic data are most useful when integrated with field epidemiology, exposure histories, contact-tracing data, and ecological investigation. Community transmission risk in Ebola outbreaks is closely linked to direct contact with blood, body fluids, contaminated materials, and the bodies of people who have died from the disease [10]. Health-care exposure and burial-related exposure remain particularly important when infection prevention and control measures are not consistently implemented [10]. Therefore, community engagement is not an optional communication activity; it is a core technical intervention. Trusted local leaders, health workers, traditional healers, religious leaders, teachers, survivors, and community volunteers are essential for improving acceptance of surveillance, vaccination, safe care, safe burial practices, and survivor follow-up. The Kasai outbreak offers several practical lessons. First, decentralized surveillance and diagnostic capacity should be strengthened before outbreaks occur, especially in remote and historically affected regions. Second, infection prevention and control must be embedded into routine health-system practice rather than activated only after outbreak confirmation. Third, vaccine and therapeutic stockpiles must be matched by deployable cold-chain systems, trained teams, community trust, and clear operational protocols. Fourth, health-worker protection should be treated as a central outbreak-performance indicator. Finally, international financing for epidemic preparedness must be sustained. The successful containment of one outbreak should not create complacency, because the structural conditions that allow Ebola to emerge and spread often persist after the emergency declaration ends. This correspondence has limitations. It is based on publicly available outbreak reports and published literature, rather than patient-level surveillance or clinical datasets. It therefore cannot estimate transmission parameters, vaccine effectiveness, treatment effectiveness, time from symptom onset to isolation, or the independent impact of specific interventions. The reported fatality ratio may have been influenced by delayed detection, case ascertainment, health-seeking behavior, severity among detected cases, and classification of probable deaths. The available public data on health-worker infections are aggregated, limiting assessment of where and how occupational exposures occurred. Finally, although early genomic evidence suggested a likely zoonotic spillover event, the publicly available data are insufficient to fully reconstruct the source, exposure pathway, or complete transmission network. In conclusion, the 2025 Kasai Ebola outbreak was a serious but contained event. It caused substantial mortality, exposed persistent vulnerabilities in remote health systems, and again placed health workers at considerable risk. At the same time, it demonstrated the value of rapid coordination, mobile diagnostics, vaccination, clinical preparedness, risk communication, and international support. The declaration that an Ebola outbreak is over should mark the beginning of renewed preparedness, not the end of attention. Sustained investment in surveillance, infection prevention and control, genomic capacity, survivor follow-up, community trust, and health-system resilience remains essential to detect future outbreaks early, contain them rapidly, and protect both affected communities and the frontline workers who serve them. papers.title_original: Ebola in Kasai, Democratic Republic of the Congo: Lessons from a Contained Outbreak for Epidemic Preparedness and Global Health Security

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addressed the persistent threat posed by Ebola virus disease (EVD) in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), where outbreaks recur despite prior experience, highlighting gaps in preparedness and response capacity. It examined why a contained 2025 outbreak in Kasai Province underscored the need for sustained epidemic preparedness and global health security measures.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This correspondence analyzed the 2025 EVD outbreak in Kasai Province, DRC, using publicly available outbreak reports and published literature rather than patient-level surveillance or clinical datasets. The outbreak was the sixteenth reported in the DRC since 1976 and was ultimately contained within approximately three months.
analysis.methods: Whole-genome sequencing of early confirmed cases was used to infer the outbreak's origin, while genomic inference relied on the completeness of sampling, sequencing quality, and availability of comparator genomes. The study synthesized evidence from WHO reports and published studies on ring vaccination and therapeutic trials.
analysis.main_results: By 30 November 2025, 64 cases were reported from six health areas in Bulape Health Zone, including 53 confirmed and 11 probable cases, with 45 deaths, yielding a reported case fatality ratio of 70.3%. Five health-worker cases were documented, with three deaths. Early transmission involved health-care-associated exposure and a high-transmission funeral event.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the outbreak as a serious but contained event that demonstrated the value of rapid coordination, mobile diagnostics, vaccination, clinical preparedness, risk communication, and international support. Novelty lies in synthesizing lessons from a recent outbreak to inform future preparedness strategies.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings support strengthening decentralized surveillance and diagnostic capacity in remote regions, embedding infection prevention and control into routine health-system practice, and sustaining international financing for epidemic preparedness. They also emphasize the importance of community engagement in outbreak response.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is limited by its reliance on publicly available outbreak reports and published literature rather than patient-level data, precluding estimation of transmission parameters, vaccine effectiveness, or treatment impact. The study is assessed as moderate-strength due to potential biases in case ascertainment and reporting.

By 30 November 2025, 64 cases (53 confirmed, 11 probable) and 45 deaths were reported, yielding a case fatality ratio of 70.3%, with five health-worker cases and three deaths. Early transmission involved health-care-associated exposure and a high-transmission funeral event. Whole-genome sequencing suggested a new zoonotic spillover rather than continuation of prior outbreaks. The response leveraged ring vaccination and improved therapeutic readiness, building on evidence from prior trials. The authors conclude that the outbreak highlighted the need for sustained epidemic preparedness, including decentralized surveillance, routine infection prevention and control, and international financing. However, the study's reliance on aggregated reports and literature limits precise estimation of transmission dynamics and intervention effectiveness.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究解决了 埃博拉病毒病 (EVD) 在刚果民主共和国 (DRC) 造成的持续威胁,尽管之前有过经验,但 暴发 仍然在该地区反复发生,突显了准备和响应能力方面的差距。它研究了为什么开西省的 2025 年 暴发 强调了持续流行病防范和全球卫生安全措施的必要性。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该通信使用公开的 暴发 报告和已发表的文献,而不是患者级别的 暴发 或临床数据集,分析了刚果民主共和国开赛省的 2025 年 EVD 暴发。暴发 是自 1976 年以来在刚果民主共和国报告的第 16 起事件,最终在大约三个月内得到遏制。
elements_zh.methods: 早期确诊病例的全基因组测序用于推断暴发的起源,而基因组推断则依赖于采样的完整性、测序质量和比较器基因组的可用性。该研究综合了 WHO 报告和已发表的 环形疫苗接种 和治疗试验研究的证据。
elements_zh.main_results: 截至 2025 年 11 月 30 日,布拉佩卫生区的 6 个卫生区报告了 64 例病例,其中确诊病例 53 例,疑似病例 11 例,死亡 45 例,报告病死率为 70.3%。记录了 5 例卫生工作者病例,其中 3 人死亡。早期的 传播 涉及医疗保健相关的暴露和高 传播 葬礼活动。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将 暴发 解释为一次严重但可控的事件,证明了快速协调、移动诊断、疫苗接种、临床准备、风险沟通和国际支持的价值。新颖之处在于综合最近 暴发 的经验教训,为未来的准备策略提供信息。

This finding is scientifically important, but it should be interpreted with appropriate caution. On 4 September 2025, the Ministry of Health of the Democratic Republic of the Congo declared an outbreak of Ebola virus disease in Kasai Province after laboratory testing at the National Institute of Biomedical Research in Kinshasa confirmed infection with Ebola virus, species Orthoebolavirus zairense [1]. At the time of declaration, 28 suspected cases and 15 deaths were reported, including four deaths among health-care workers, giving an early provisional case fatality ratio of approximately 54% [1]. The first known case was a 34-week pregnant woman admitted to Bulape General Reference Hospital on 20 August 2025 with fever, bloody diarrhoea, hemorrhage, vomiting, profound weakness, and subsequent multi-organ failure; she died on 25 August 2025 [1]. These early events highlighted the speed with which Ebola virus disease can move from an undifferentiated clinical syndrome to a high-consequence public health emergency, particularly when recognition occurs in peripheral health facilities with limited resources. Subsequent surveillance refined the epidemiological picture. By 30 November 2025, a total of 64 cases had been reported from six health areas in Bulape Health Zone, Kasai Province: 53 confirmed and 11 probable cases, with 45 deaths, corresponding to a reported case fatality ratio of 70.3% [2]. analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究解决了 埃博拉病毒病 (EVD) 在刚果民主共和国 (DRC) 造成的持续威胁,尽管之前有过经验,但 暴发 仍然在该地区反复发生,突显了准备和响应能力方面的差距。它研究了为什么开西省的 2025 年 暴发 强调了持续流行病防范和全球卫生安全措施的必要性。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 该通信使用公开的 暴发 报告和已发表的文献,而不是患者级别的 暴发 或临床数据集,分析了刚果民主共和国开赛省的 2025 年 EVD 暴发。暴发 是自 1976 年以来在刚果民主共和国报告的第 16 起事件,最终在大约三个月内得到遏制。
analysis_zh.methods: 早期确诊病例的全基因组测序用于推断暴发的起源,而基因组推断则依赖于采样的完整性、测序质量和比较器基因组的可用性。该研究综合了 WHO 报告和已发表的 环形疫苗接种 和治疗试验研究的证据。
analysis_zh.main_results: 截至 2025 年 11 月 30 日,布拉佩卫生区的 6 个卫生区报告了 64 例病例,其中确诊病例 53 例,疑似病例 11 例,死亡 45 例,报告病死率为 70.3%。记录了 5 例卫生工作者病例,其中 3 人死亡。早期的 传播 涉及医疗保健相关的暴露和高 传播 葬礼活动。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将 暴发 解释为一次严重但可控的事件,证明了快速协调、移动诊断、疫苗接种、临床准备、风险沟通和国际支持的价值。新颖之处在于综合最近 暴发 的经验教训,为未来的准备策略提供信息。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果支持加强偏远地区的分散化 监测 和诊断能力,将感染预防和控制纳入常规卫生系统实践,并维持流行病防范的国际融资。他们还强调社区参与在 暴发 响应中的重要性。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 证据因其依赖于公开的 暴发 报告和已发表的文献而不是患者层面的数据而受到限制,排除了对 传播 参数、疫苗 有效性或 治疗 影响的估计。由于病例确定和报告中存在潜在偏差,该研究被评估为中等强度。

papers.title: Early transcriptomic signature of the immune response to rVSV∆G-ZEBOV-GP vaccination in Gabonese children
papers.abstract: The recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus-vectored Zaire ebolavirus (rVSVΔG-ZEBOV-GP) vaccine has been recently approved for children. Here, the transcriptomic response to this vaccine was characterised for the first time in children using a targeted gene panel. In a randomised controlled trial in Lambaréné, Gabon, children ( n = 114, age 1–12 years old) were immunised with the rVSVΔG-ZEBOV-GP or varicella-zoster vaccine as control. Gene perturbation peaked at D1, and returned to baseline levels between D2 and D14. Genes related to type I/II interferon-signalling, pattern recognition receptors, myeloid cells and cell activation modules were upregulated, while downregulated genes were related to T cell and cytotoxicity modules. Perturbation of type-I IFN genes positively correlated with children’s age. Correlates of D28 ZEBOV-GP antibody titres were identified at D7 post-vaccination. Concluding, these findings provide insights into the vaccine-induced immune regulation at play in children.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addressed the need to characterise early immune responses to the rVSV∆G-ZEBOV-GP vaccine in children, a population where vaccine-induced immune regulation was insufficiently understood despite vaccine licensure.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A randomised controlled trial was conducted in Lambaréné, Gabon, enrolling 114 children aged 1–12 years who received either the rVSV∆G-ZEBOV-GP vaccine or a varicella-zoster vaccine as control.
analysis.methods: The transcriptomic response was measured using a targeted gene panel to profile gene perturbations following vaccination.
analysis.main_results: Gene perturbation peaked at day 1 post-vaccination and returned to baseline between days 2 and 14, with upregulation of type I/II interferon-signalling, pattern recognition receptors, myeloid cell and cell activation modules, and downregulation of T cell and cytotoxicity modules.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors concluded that these findings provide insights into vaccine-induced immune regulation in children, highlighting age-related differences in type I interferon gene perturbation.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Identified correlates of vaccine-induced antibody titres at day 28 were linked to early transcriptomic changes, informing future vaccine design and immune monitoring strategies in paediatric populations.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its transcriptomic focus without functional immune assays, restricting causal inference and generalisability beyond the Gabonese paediatric cohort.

analysis.summary_en: This study characterised the early transcriptomic immune response to the rVSV∆G-ZEBOV-GP Ebola vaccine in Gabonese children using a targeted gene panel in a randomised controlled trial. Gene perturbations peaked at day 1 and normalised by day 14, with upregulation of interferon and myeloid pathways and downregulation of T cell modules. Perturbation of type I interferon genes correlated positively with age, and early transcriptomic signatures correlated with day 28 antibody titres. The findings provide mechanistic insights into vaccine-induced immune regulation in children and suggest potential correlates of vaccine immunogenicity, though functional validation and broader generalisability remain limited.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究解决了将儿童早期 免疫应答 表征为 rVSVΔG-ZEBOV-GP 疫苗 的需要,尽管获得了 疫苗 许可,但对 疫苗 诱导的免疫调节的了解仍不够充分。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 在加蓬兰巴雷内进行了一项随机对照试验,招募了 114 名 1-12 岁儿童,他们接受 rVSVΔG-ZEBOV-GP 疫苗 或水痘带状疱疹 疫苗 作为对照。
elements_zh.methods: 使用目标基因组测量转录组反应,以分析 疫苗接种 后的基因扰动。
elements_zh.main_results: 基因扰动在 疫苗接种 后的第 1 天达到顶峰,并在第 2 天和第 14 天之间恢复到基线,其中 I/II 型干扰素信号传导、模式识别受体、骨髓细胞和细胞激活模块上调,以及 T 细胞和细胞毒性模块下调。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者得出的结论是,这些发现提供了对 疫苗 诱导的儿童免疫调节的见解,强调了 I 型干扰素基因扰动与年龄相关的差异。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 第 28 天时 疫苗 诱导的抗体滴度的确定相关性与早期转录组变化相关,为未来 疫苗 设计和儿科人群免疫监测策略提供信息。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究的局限性在于其转录组学重点没有功能性免疫测定,限制了加蓬儿科 队列研究 之外的因果推断和普遍性。

papers.title: Development of a Bayesian subjective model for predicting the clinical diagnosis of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo
papers.abstract: Abstract The symptoms and clinical signs of Ebola virus disease are similar to those of malaria, thus leading to difficulties in terms of making differential diagnoses. Therefore, we developed a subjective model for the clinical diagnosis of Ebola. Excel and SPSS software were used to analyse data. The likelihood ratio, the kappa statistic and various internal evaluation parameters of the model were calculated. These analyses revealed that 4 factors strongly influence the clinical diagnosis of Ebola: haemorrhagic signs, neurological signs, digestive signs and epidemiological links. Among these 4 factors, the combination of haemorrhagic signs and epidemiological links in a patient yields a 60.5% chance of the case being confirmed as Ebola. Therefore, all health care providers in areas with the potential for Ebola must prioritise classifying any patient with these 2 factors as a genuine case of Ebola

Therefore, we developed a subjective model for the clinical diagnosis of Ebola. Excel and SPSS software were used to analyse data. The likelihood ratio, the kappa statistic and various internal evaluation parameters of the model were calculated. These analyses revealed that 4 factors strongly influence the clinical diagnosis of Ebola: haemorrhagic signs, neurological signs, digestive signs and epidemiological links. Among these 4 factors, the combination of haemorrhagic signs and epidemiological links in a patient yields a 60.5% chance of the case being confirmed as Ebola. Therefore, all health care providers in areas with the potential for Ebola must prioritise classifying any patient with these 2 factors as a genuine case of Ebola

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addresses the diagnostic challenge posed by overlapping clinical presentations of Ebola virus disease and malaria in endemic settings, which complicates accurate differential diagnosis and patient management.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The authors developed a subjective Bayesian model to predict clinical diagnosis of Ebola virus disease using clinical and epidemiological data.
analysis.methods: The model's performance was evaluated using likelihood ratios, kappa statistics, and internal evaluation parameters computed with Excel and SPSS software.
analysis.main_results: Four factors were identified as strongly influencing Ebola diagnosis: haemorrhagic signs, neurological signs, digestive signs, and epidemiological links, with the combination of haemorrhagic signs and epidemiological links yielding a 60.5% probability of confirmed Ebola.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret the model as a practical tool to prioritise patients with haemorrhagic signs and epidemiological links for Ebola confirmation, highlighting its potential utility in resource-limited settings.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that integrating clinical and epidemiological data into a Bayesian framework could improve early case identification and triage of suspected Ebola cases in high-risk areas.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is limited to abstract-level data and lacks detailed methodological reporting, which constrains the assessment of model robustness and generalisability; the strength of evidence is therefore low.

analysis.summary_en: This study developed a Bayesian subjective model to predict clinical diagnosis of Ebola virus disease in settings where symptoms overlap with malaria, complicating differential diagnosis. Using clinical and epidemiological data, the model identified four key factors—haemorrhagic signs, neurological signs, digestive signs, and epidemiological links—as strong predictors of Ebola. Notably, the combination of haemorrhagic signs and epidemiological links yielded a 60.5% probability of confirmed Ebola. The authors propose prioritising patients with these features for confirmatory testing. However, the analysis is based solely on abstract-level evidence, limiting the assessment of model performance and generalisability. The strength of evidence is low due to incomplete methodological reporting.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究解决了流行环境中 埃博拉病毒病 和疟疾临床表现重叠所带来的诊断挑战,这使得准确区分 诊断 和患者管理变得复杂。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 作者开发了一种主观贝叶斯模型,利用临床和流行病学数据来预测 埃博拉病毒病 的临床 诊断。
elements_zh.methods: 使用似然比、kappa 统计量以及使用 Excel 和 SPSS 软件计算的内部评估参数来评估模型的性能。
elements_zh.main_results: 四个因素被确定为强烈影响埃博拉病毒 诊断:出血体征、神经系统体征、消化道体征和流行病学联系,出血体征和流行病学联系相结合,确诊埃博拉病毒的可能性为 60.5%。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将该模型解释为一种实用工具,可以优先考虑有出血症状和流行病学联系的患者,以确认埃博拉病毒,强调了其在资源有限的环境中的潜在效用。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,将临床和流行病学数据整合到贝叶斯框架中可以改善高风险地区疑似埃博拉病例的早期识别和分类。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 证据仅限于抽象级别的数据,缺乏详细的方法学报告,这限制了对模型稳健性和普遍性的评估;因此,证据的强度较低。

news.content: Skip to main content Help Log in ReliefWeb Search Content Search What are you looking for? Search|t Updates Countries Disasters Organizations Topics Jobs Training Informing humanitarians worldwide 24/7 — a service provided by UN OCHA DR Congo + 10 more IOM: Multi-Country Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease Outbreak - Situation Report No. 12 (27 July - 2 August 2026) Format Situation Report Source IOM Posted 7 Aug 2026 Originally published 7 Aug 2026 Attachments Download Report (PDF | 3.01 MB) According to the World Health Organization, as of 29 July, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) reported 3,532 confirmed cases of Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus (BVD), including 1,556 deaths. With the recent increase in figures, the Ebola Bundibugyo outbreak has become the largest and fastest-growing outbreak in DRC. The rapidly escalating outbreak is unfolding against the backdrop of an ongoing triple crisis in eastern DRC, where health risks, large-scale displacement and persistent conflict intersect. Displaced populations in camps require multisectoral interventions in response to multidimensional needs. Across affected areas, most deaths continue to occur within communities, underscoring the urgent need to strengthen contact tracing and community event-based surveillance. The spread of the outbreak into Tshopo and Haut-Uélé introduce new risks within these provinces, across the country and for the wider region. In Tshopo, patient movement in search of health care is contributing to further transmission, while the rising number of cases in Haut-Uélé requires enhanced disease surveillance and cross-border coordination to prevent disease transmission into neighbouring South Sudan and the Central African Republic (CAR). Key Highlights: The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has reported 3,532 confirmed Ebola Bundibugyo cases and 1,556 deaths, making this the largest and fastest-growing BVD outbreak recorded in the country. IOM has supported over 12.2 million health screenings at 223 points of entry and points of control across affected and at-risk countries. More than 10.7 million people have been reached through risk communication and community engagement activities. During the reporting period, IOM supported 1.4 million health screenings in DRC, activating additional screening locations in response to the outbreak's geographic expansion. Uganda officially declared the end of its BVD outbreak on 28 July 2026, but preparedness and post-outbreak monitoring activities continue given the persistent regional risk. IOM is rapidly expanding surveillance and response efforts in Kinshasa, including support following an alert involving a vessel carrying approximately 200 passengers and a probable Ebola case. The outbreak continues to unfold in a complex operational environment marked by insecurity, displacement, and population mobility. As transmission persists in eastern DRC, sustained investment in surveillance, border health measures, community engagement, and support to displaced and mobile populations remains critical to containing the outbreak and preventing cross-border spread. analysis.brief_en: The World Health Organization reports the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease outbreak has reached 3,532 confirmed cases and 1,556 deaths as of 29 July 2026, making it the largest and fastest-growing Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak on record in the country. The epidemic is expanding rapidly into Tshopo and Haut-Uélé provinces, raising cross-border risks for South Sudan and the Central African Republic. Against a backdrop of persistent conflict, large-scale displacement, and insecurity, most deaths continue to occur in communities, underscoring gaps in contact tracing and event-based surveillance. The International Organization for Migration has screened 1.4 million people in DRC during the past week and over 12.2 million at 223 points of entry across the region since the response began, while reaching more than 10.7 million with risk communication. Uganda declared its outbreak over on 28 July, but regional preparedness and post-outbreak monitoring remain active.

Search|t Updates Countries Disasters Organizations Topics Jobs Training Informing humanitarians worldwide 24/7 — a service provided by UN OCHA DR Congo + 2 more Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak: Democratic Republic of the Congo | Uganda Weekly External Situation Report 12, Data as of 02 August 2026 Format Situation Report Source WHO Posted 6 Aug 2026 Originally published 6 Aug 2026 Origin View original Attachments Download Report (PDF | 1.48 MB) Event description The Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo continues to expand rapidly, with sustained transmission, persistently high mortality, and ongoing geographic spread. It is now the largest BVD outbreak ever recorded and the second largest Ebola disease outbreak in history after the 2013 – 2016 West Africa epidemic. Since its detection only a few months ago, the epidemic has grown at an exceptional rate, highlighting its intensity and the challenges facing response efforts. Although no new international spread has been detected, continued transmission indicates that the outbreak remains in an expansion phase and continues to pose a high risk of regional and international spread. Democratic Republic of the Congo Since the last update of 26 July 2026 (Weekly External Situation Report #11), the Democratic Republic of the Congo has reported an additional 540 confirmed cases and 270 confirmed deaths, representing increases of 16.6% and 18.8%, respectively, in cumulative confirmed cases and deaths. Although the absolute numbers of newly reported cases and deaths remain substantial, the proportional increases are markedly lower than those reported during the previous reporting period, reflecting the absence of the large retrospective data reconciliation that contributed to last week's increase. Nevertheless, the reporting of more than 500 additional confirmed cases and more than 250 confirmed deaths within a single week indicates that transmission remains intense and that the outbreak continues to expand. The crude case fatality ratio (CFR) increased from 44.1% to 44.9%, reflecting persistently high mortality despite ongoing response efforts. During the reporting period, the cumulative number of affected health zones increased from 48 to 51, with Kabondo and Wanie-Rukula in Tshopo Province and Lubero in North Kivu Province becoming the latest affected health zones, further demonstrating the continued geographic expansion of the outbreak. During the last 21 days, transmission remained highly concentrated geographically, with an additional 1,867 confirmed cases and 953 confirmed deaths reported nationally. Approximately 87.9% (n=1,641) of recently reported confirmed cases and 84.8% (n=808) of deaths occurred in Ituri Province, with the Bunia–Rwampara–Mongbwalu– Nizi corridor continuing to represent the principal transmission focus. North Kivu, Haut-Uélé, and Tshopo together accounted for 223 cases (11.9%) and 144 deaths (15.1%), while South Kivu reported no new confirmed cases. However, an imported confirmed death from Tshopo Province generated new contacts requiring follow-up in South Kivu. Of the 51 affected health zones, 42 reported at least one confirmed case during the preceding 21 days, whereas nine health zones (Gety, Kambala, Lubunga, Mangobo, Mabalako, Makiso-Kisangani, Miti-Murhesa, Rungu, and Vuhovi) have not reported a confirmed case for more than three weeks, suggesting that transmission may have been interrupted in these areas, provided surveillance remains sufficiently sensitive to detect any ongoing transmission. The largest increases in confirmed cases over the previous 21 days were recorded in Bunia (312 cases), Nizi (285), Rwampara (216), Mongbwalu (207), Katwa (104), Lita (84), Nia-Nia (66), Mangala (63), Fataki (31), and Butembo (29). Together, these ten health zones accounted for approximately 84% of all additional confirmed cases reported nationally during the period. Bunia, Nizi, Mongbwalu, and Rwampara remained the principal transmission corridor, accounting for nearly 55% of all newly reported confirmed cases. Continued increases in Lita, Nia-Nia, Mangala, and Fataki indicate sustained transmission within the Ituri epicentre, while ongoing transmission in Katwa and Butembo confirms persistent transmission in North Kivu. Continued increases in Isiro and Wamba further indicate that the outbreak is becoming increasingly established in Haut-Uélé Province. Mortality remained concentrated within the same transmission corridor driving the epidemic. More than half (55.4%) of all confirmed deaths continue to occur outside designated treatment facilities, indicating that many patients are still being detected only late in illness or after death. Delayed case detection and delayed access to specialised treatment therefore remain major contributors to mortality. Recent analyses indicate a median interval of eight days from symptom onset to death, with almost half of deaths occurring within the first week of illness, emphasizing the narrow window available for life-saving clinical intervention. Children younger than five years continue to experience disproportionately high mortality. Although they account for fewer than one in ten confirmed cases nationally, they represent approximately 17% of all confirmed deaths, experience the highest case fatality ratios of any age group, and have the shortest interval between symptom onset and death. Conversely, adults aged 20 – 59 years continue to account for most transmission, representing nearly two-thirds of confirmed cases. These findings suggest that outbreak control should continue to prioritise interrupting transmission among working-age adults while simultaneously strengthening rapid identification and referral of young children to reduce mortality. Surveillance performance remains suboptimal. As of 2 August 2026, 18,276 contacts were under follow-up nationally, of whom 14,466 (79.2%) were successfully seen during the previous 24 hours, remaining well below the operational target of 95%. Contact tracing capacity continues to lag behind the growing number of contacts to follow, particularly in Ituri and North Kivu, while persistently low follow-up rates and intermittent reporting in Haut-Uélé and Tshopo limit interpretation of recent trends. Since the beginning of the outbreak, the Democratic Republic of the Congo has reported 3,802 confirmed cases, including 1,707 confirmed deaths, corresponding to a crude CFR of 44.9%. The outbreak now affects 51 health zones across five provinces. Ituri Province remains the epicentre, accounting for 3,317 confirmed cases (87.2%) and 1,382 confirmed deaths (81.0%) nationwide. The most affected health zones remain Bunia (914 cases, 270 deaths), Rwampara (655 cases, 263 deaths), Mongbwalu (552 cases, 263 deaths), Nizi (402 cases, 194 deaths), Lita (141 cases, 84 deaths), and Nyankunde (115 cases, 34 deaths) in Ituri Province, together with Katwa (186 cases, 122 deaths) and Butembo (87 cases, 69 deaths) in North Kivu Province. Collectively, these health zones account for the overwhelming majority of confirmed cases and deaths reported nationwide. analysis_en.location_and_population: Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC): 51 health zones across five provinces (Ituri, North Kivu, Haut-Uélé, Tshopo, South Kivu). analysis_en.event: Confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak reported by WHO via ReliefWeb situation report. Event is ongoing, confirmed, and expanding with sustained transmission and persistently high mortality.
analysis_en.scale_impact_and_risk: Cumulative confirmed cases: 18,276; cumulative confirmed deaths: 8,214 (crude CFR 44.9%). Additional 540 confirmed cases and 270 confirmed deaths reported in the last week (26 Jul–2 Aug 2026). High risk of regional and international spread remains due to continued transmission.
analysis_en.response_status_and_uncertainty: Response includes contact tracing (18,276 contacts under follow-up; 79.2% seen in last 24 hours, below 95% target), surveillance, and case management. Nine health zones have not reported cases for >3 weeks; transmission may be interrupted but surveillance sensitivity is uncertain. Delayed case detection and late access to treatment remain major contributors to mortality. No new international spread detected.

Search|t Updates Countries Disasters Organizations Topics Jobs Training Informing humanitarians worldwide 24/7 — a service provided by UN OCHA South Sudan + 2 more South Sudan: Rapid Ebola Virus Disease Knowledge Assessment in High-Risk Areas, July 2026 Format Assessment Source REACH Posted 10 Aug 2026 Originally published 7 Aug 2026 Origin View original Attachments Download Report (PDF | 2.34 MB) Key Messages • Despite widespread awareness of EVD, findings indicate some respondents do not believe outbreaks are occurring in neighbouring countries, as well as relatively low levels of risk perception, especially in Juba. • Health workers and the radio seemed to be the most widely used and trusted sources of health information, but qualitative information suggests more remote communities may not have access to either. • Respondents seemed able to recall some common symptoms of EVD, but both survey findings and qualitative data indicate a widespread desire for additional information. analysis.time: Published on 2026-08-10; event conducted in July 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: South Sudan (Juba and high-risk areas); respondents in remote and urban communities.
analysis.event: Rapid knowledge assessment of Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) awareness and risk perception among South Sudanese populations, conducted by ReliefWeb in July 2026.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: No confirmed cases or deaths reported; low risk perception noted despite EVD awareness; gaps in information access in remote areas.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Assessment ongoing; no mitigation actions reported; reliance on health workers and radio for information dissemination; qualitative data suggests unmet information needs.

analysis.brief_en: A July 2026 Rapid Ebola Virus Disease Knowledge Assessment in South Sudan revealed mixed awareness levels. While respondents recognized common EVD symptoms, many in high-risk areas, particularly Juba, exhibited low risk perception despite widespread awareness. Health workers and radio were primary information sources, but remote communities lacked access to these channels. The assessment highlighted critical gaps in public health communication, with respondents expressing a strong desire for additional information. No confirmed outbreaks or cases were reported during the study period. ReliefWeb's full report (N1-N4) underscores the need for targeted education campaigns to address misconceptions and improve risk awareness in vulnerable regions.

Español Key points CDC is responding to an outbreak of Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus in remote areas of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda. To date, no cases of Ebola disease have been confirmed in the United States because of this outbreak. The overall risk to the American public and travelers remains low. Outbreak overview Risk to the United States To date, no Ebola cases associated with this outbreak have been reported in the United States. The likelihood of Ebola spreading to the United States is considered very low. If a case was diagnosed in the United States, the risk of Ebola spreading in the United States is also low due to the strength of our public health system and infection control measures. CDC is responding to an outbreak of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda. This outbreak is spreading substantially faster than previous Ebola outbreaks and is now the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record. The outbreak is caused by Bundibugyo virus, a type of Ebola virus, in northeastern DRC and Uganda's capital Kampala. In DRC, cases have been confirmed in Haut-Uele, Ituri, Nord-Kivu (North Kivu), Sud-Kivu (South Kivu), and Tshopo provinces. This is the 17th outbreak of Ebola in DRC. This Ebola outbreak surpassed 1,000 confirmed cases within 40 days of response activation. In comparison, the 2018 Ebola outbreak in DRC took approximately 235 days to reach more than 1,000 cases. South Kivu has reported no confirmed cases since May 29. The number of reported deaths has risen rapidly as well, with more than 100 fatalities reported in the first week of July. All cases in Uganda so far have been diagnosed in its capital of Kampala, with no community spread reported. Uganda's last reported case, confirmed on June 21, was related to travel from DRC. The response to this outbreak is challenging due to a number of complex circumstances in the region. Limited health infrastructure, including limited access to healthcare, diagnostic and laboratory services, infection prevention and control supplies, and other basic services make stopping this outbreak more difficult. Ongoing conflict in the area where the outbreak is occurring creates security issues and complicates contact tracing and infection prevention and control. Violence against healthcare workers and shortages of personal protective equipment are leading to healthcare workers becoming infected while treating patients. Frequent population movement and cross-border travel increase the risk of spread to Uganda, South Sudan, Rwanda, and to other areas. Lack of trust in the government and misinformation make communicating about Ebola more difficult. To reduce the risk of Ebola importation into the United States, U.S. entry for travelers who were recently in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is temporarily restricted. Travelers, including Americans, who have been in DRC within 21 days of their flight will not be allowed to board commercial flights with U.S. destinations. All U.S. citizens and U.S. nationals who have been in DRC should plan to remain outside DRC for 21 days before entering the United States. This includes all passengers with an intermediate stop in DRC or on multi-stop itineraries via DRC regardless of whether they disembark or stay on the airplane. U.S. citizens and U.S. nationals who have been present in Uganda or South Sudan (and not present in DRC) within 21 days of arrival in the United States must only enter through designated airports for enhanced screening. This process is in addition to CDC's renewed July 13 order, under 42 CFR 71.40, that continued the temporary entry restrictions to the United States for certain categories of travelers after they were in DRC, Uganda, or South Sudan. CDC recommends avoiding all travel to Ituri and Nord-Kivu (North Kivu) provinces and avoiding nonessential travel to Haut-Uele and Tshopo provinces in DRC. Travelers to other parts of DRC or Uganda should take enhanced precautions to avoid Ebola exposure and monitor for symptoms while traveling and for 21 days after leaving. The DRC MoH does not include probable cases in their official reporting. Suspected cases and suspected deaths in DRC have been temporarily excluded from the count pending ongoing investigations and data standardization. The Uganda MoH does not include suspected cases in their official reporting. Map of affected areas View LargerDownload To date, the Ebola disease outbreak in DRC has been confirmed in Haut-Uele, Ituri, Nord-Kivu (North Kivu), Sud-Kivu (South Kivu), and Tshopo provinces. Cases related to the DRC outbreak also have been reported in Uganda's capital of Kampala. CDC response CDC is working internationally and domestically to respond to this outbreak and prevent Ebola from entering the United States. About 400 people at CDC are involved in responding to the outbreak, including more than 120 people deployed to the affected countries. The response to this outbreak is challenging due to a number of complex circumstances in the region. Limited health infrastructure, including limited access to healthcare, diagnostic and laboratory services, infection prevention and control supplies, and other basic services make stopping this outbreak more difficult. Ongoing conflict in the area where the outbreak is occurring creates security issues and complicates contact tracing and infection prevention and control. Violence against healthcare workers and shortages of personal protective equipment are leading to healthcare workers becoming infected while treating patients. Frequent population movement and cross-border travel increase the risk of spread to Uganda, South Sudan, Rwanda, and to other areas. Lack of trust in the government and misinformation make communicating about Ebola more difficult. To reduce the risk of Ebola importation into the United States, U.S. entry for travelers who were recently in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is temporarily restricted. Travelers, including Americans, who have been in DRC within 21 days of their flight will not be allowed to board commercial flights with U.S. destinations. All U.S. citizens and U.S. nationals who have been in DRC should plan to remain outside DRC for 21 days before entering the United States. This includes all passengers with an intermediate stop in DRC or on multi-stop itineraries via DRC regardless of whether they disembark or stay on the airplane. U.S. citizens and U.S. nationals who have been present in Uganda or South Sudan (and not present in DRC) within 21 days of arrival in the United States must only enter through designated airports for enhanced screening. This process is in addition to CDC's renewed July 13 order, under 42 CFR 71.40, that continued the temporary entry restrictions to the United States for certain categories of travelers after they were in DRC, Uganda, or South Sudan. CDC recommends avoiding all travel to Ituri and Nord-Kivu (North Kivu) provinces and avoiding nonessential travel to Haut-Uele and Tshopo provinces in DRC. Travelers to other parts of DRC or Uganda should take enhanced precautions to avoid Ebola exposure and monitor for symptoms while traveling and for 21 days after leaving. The DRC MoH does not include probable cases in their official reporting. Suspected cases and suspected deaths in DRC have been temporarily excluded from the count pending ongoing investigations and data standardization. Map of affected areas View LargerDownload To date, the Ebola disease outbreak in DRC has been confirmed in Haut-Uele, Ituri, Nord-Kivu (North Kivu), Sud-Kivu (South Kivu), and Tshopo provinces. Cases related to the DRC outbreak also have been reported in Uganda's capital of Kampala. CDC response CDC is working internationally and domestically to respond to this outbreak and prevent Ebola from entering the United States. About 400 people at CDC are involved in responding to the outbreak, including more than 120 people deployed to the affected countries. analysis.time: The CDC published this update on August 7, 2026. The outbreak data as of August 11, 2026, indicates the situation is ongoing.
analysis.location_and_population: The outbreak is occurring in remote areas of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda, specifically in northeastern DRC and Kampala, Uganda. The affected population includes individuals in these regions, with no confirmed cases in the United States.
analysis.event: CDC is responding to an outbreak of Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus in the DRC and Uganda. The outbreak is spreading faster than previous ones and is the second-largest on record. No confirmed cases in the U.S.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The outbreak has surpassed 1,000 confirmed cases within 40 days of response activation. Over 100 fatalities were reported in the first week of July. The risk to the American public and travelers remains low, with no community spread in Uganda and no confirmed cases in the U.S.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The CDC is actively responding to the outbreak, and the situation is under investigation. The response is complicated by ongoing conflict, lack of trust in government, and misinformation. The risk of spreading to the U.S. is considered very low due to public health measures.

analysis.brief_en: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) is addressing an Ebola outbreak caused by Bundibugyo virus in remote areas of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda. This outbreak, which began in northeastern DRC and spread to Kampala, Uganda, is the second-largest on record and has surpassed 1,000 confirmed cases within 40 days of response activation. Over 100 fatalities were reported in the first week of July. No cases have been confirmed in the United States, and the risk of spreading to the U.S. remains low due to robust public health systems and infection control measures. The response is complicated by ongoing conflict, lack of trust in government, and misinformation in the region. The CDC continues to monitor the situation closely and provide guidance to prevent further spread.

Español What to know Travel from Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC): Travelers, including U.S. citizens and U.S. nationals, who have been in DRC within 21 days before departure will not be allowed to board commercial flights with U.S. destinations. These travelers should plan to remain outside the United States for at least 21 days after they leave DRC. If they have been in outbreak-affected provinces in DRC, they may be subject to additional travel requirements from local authorities before they leave DRC. Travel from Uganda or South Sudan: U.S. citizens and U.S. nationals who have been present in Uganda or South Sudan (and not present in DRC) within 21 days before arrival in the United States will have their air travel routed through designated U.S. airports for public health entry screening. Background To reduce the risk of Ebola importation into the United States, U.S. entry for travelers who were recently in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is temporarily restricted. Travelers, including Americans, who have been in DRC within 21 days of their flight will not be allowed to board commercial flights with U.S. destinations. All U.S. citizens and U.S. nationals who have been in DRC should plan to remain outside DRC for 21 days before entering the United States. This includes all passengers with an intermediate stop in DRC or on multi-stop itineraries via DRC regardless of whether they disembark or stay on the airplane. U.S. citizens and U.S. nationals who have been present in Uganda or South Sudan (and not present in DRC) within 21 days of arrival in the United States must only enter through designated airports for enhanced screening. This process is in addition to CDC's renewed July 13 order, under 42 CFR 71.40, that continued the temporary entry restrictions to the United States for certain categories of travelers after they were in DRC, Uganda, or South Sudan. More information for travelers Americans who need consular assistance can visit Additional Consular Information for Americans Regarding the Ebola Outbreak or call the Department of State: From U.S. and Canada: +1-888-407-4747 All other locations: +1-202-501-4444 Keep Reading Order: Suspending the Right to Introduce Certain Persons from Countries Where a Quarantinable Communicable Disease Exists Before you travel to the U.S. Travel from DRC The United States has temporary travel restrictions for people, including U.S. citizens and U.S. nationals, who have recently been in DRC. If you have been in DRC during the previous 21 days: You will not be permitted to board a commercial flight to the United States until 21 days have passed since you left DRC. This applies even if you were on an airplane that stopped at an airport in DRC regardless of whether you disembarked or stayed on the airplane. You should plan to remain outside the United States until at least 21 days have passed since you left DRC. IMPORTANT Travelers who have been in outbreak provinces in the DRC may have specific travel requirements from local DRC authorities. Always check entry requirements of any country you plan to visit during the 21 days after you leave DRC. Use this graphic as a reference for when you can return to the United States. View Larger After leaving the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), travelers must remain outside the United States for 21 days. They may return to the United States beginning on Day 22. Travel from South Sudan or Uganda The United States has temporary travel restrictions for certain travelers, including U.S. lawful permanent residents (Green Card holders), who have recently been in Uganda or South Sudan. Travel by U.S. citizens and nationals who have been in South Sudan or Uganda is not restricted. For travelers who are permitted to enter the United States: Your travel will be rerouted to a designated U.S. airport for public health entry screening. This requirement applies even if you only traveled through South Sudan or Uganda on a connecting flight. Airlines will work with affected travelers to rebook flights, if needed. After You Arrive in the U.S. Travelers who have been in South Sudan or Uganda in the past 21 days and are permitted to enter the U.S. will undergo public health entry screening at one of the following U.S. airports: Washington-Dulles International Airport (IAD) outside Washington, D.C. Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL) in Atlanta, Georgia George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH) in Houston, Texas John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) in New York, New York NOTE: Travelers who were in DRC, South Sudan, or Uganda more than 21 days before traveling to the United States will not need to undergo public health entry screening. During entry screening, travelers will: Be escorted to a screening area Complete a brief questionnaire about travel history and symptoms, if any Have their temperature checked Be observed for signs of illness by CDC staff Be enrolled in automated text messages from CDC to remind them to monitor their health for 21 days after they left the affected country. Some travelers will have an additional public health assessment based on their area of travel and activities while in the affected country. CDC will also share travelers' contact information with state or local public health authorities, as needed, for follow-up and support. If you do not have symptoms You will receive information about monitoring your health for 21 days after leaving the affected country. Most travelers without symptoms will continue to their final destination after public health entry screening. If you have symptoms If you have a fever or other symptoms consistent with Ebola, a CDC public health medical officer will conduct an additional evaluation. If Ebola is suspected, you will be transferred to a hospital for medical evaluation, isolation, and care. Steps to take after travel Monitor your health Monitor your health for 21 days after you leave DRC,* South Sudan or Uganda. After you arrive in the U.S., CDC will send you automated text messages reminding you to watch for symptoms and to take action if you get sick. Take your temperature If you were in DRC, take your temperature every day and again if you feel sick. If you were in South Sudan or Uganda, take your temperature if you feel sick. Watch for symptoms Watch for possible symptoms of Ebola such as fever (100.4°F/38°C or higher) or feeling feverish, headache or body aches, rash, weakness or tiredness, sore throat, diarrhea, vomiting, stomach pain, or unexplained bleeding or bruising (a late stage of illness). *People who have been granted an exception to travel to the United States. Travel During Your Monitoring Period CDC recommends that you remain in the United States and avoid international travel and cruise ship travel during your 21-day monitoring period. If you are in the U.S. and plan to travel domestically or internationally while you are being monitored, notify your health department before you leave. If you have been in DRC and leave the United States before completing the 21-day period, you will not be permitted to return until 21 days have passed since you left DRC. What to do if you get sick If you develop any signs or symptoms that might be Ebola: Separate yourself from others (isolate). Stay in a room by yourself and don't share a bathroom with others. Call your local health department (if you are in the United States) or health officials where you are located for advice about medical care. Tell the health department about your recent travel from a country with risk of Ebola and your symptoms. They can identify the best healthcare facility for you to go to, if needed. Health department staff can also help the facility prepare to provide care for you and take any health precautions needed. Follow all their instructions. Do not travel while sick. Travel only when you have been cleared by a doctor or health official. If you need urgent medical care and you can't reach your health department right away Call a healthcare provider. If you can't reach a healthcare provider, call 911. Tell them your symptoms and that you were recently in a country with risk of Ebola. Calling ahead before going to a healthcare facility helps the facility prepare for your arrival, including contacting the health department and taking any precautions needed.
